utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir General Rupert Smith served in the army of the United Kingdom for 34 years. From 23 January 1995 through 20 December 1995, General Smith was the commander of the United Nations protection force or UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Every morning General Smith was briefed about the military and political events that occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the previous 24 hours. In addition to Rupert Smith's immediate staff, members of the UNHCR, the ICRC, and other agencies present in Sarajevo participated in these meetings. Every afternoon a second smaller meeting occurred, comprised of General Smith, and his headquarter staff where the events of that day -- The Court's indulgence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have the indulgence, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where the events of that day or other more long-term inquiries were discussed. General Smith also visited his sector headquarters as frequently as he could, and also exchanged information with journalists. In addition, during his tenure, General Smith met and/or had telephone conversations with military and political leaders of the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Serbs as well as leaders of the federal republic of Yugoslavia, including, Alija Izetbegovic, General Ratko Mladic, Radovan Karadzic, and Slobodan Milosevic. One of General Smith's priorities was the resolution of difficulties in implementing the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, or COHA entered into between the belligerent parties. General Smith's evidence and related documents describe a number of these discussions, the activities of UNPROFOR and NATO in Bosnia and Herzegovina during 1995, and in particular, the efforts of UNPROFOR to deliver humanitarian aide, the use of NATO air power in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1995, and how members of the army of Republika Srpska took members of UNPROFOR hostage during the spring of 1995. General Smith' evidence and associated documents discuss the shelling and sniping of civilians in the city of Sarajevo, and, in particular, the results of the UNPROFOR's investigation into the incident referred to as Markale II, which is Shelling Incident 9 in Schedule A to the indictment. General Smith's evidence describes efforts by the army of the Republika Srpska starting in late February or March 1995 to put pressure on the eastern enclaves or safe areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Srebrenica. General Smith's evidence and associated documents also describe the events in Srebrenica that occurred during July 1995 and UNPROFOR's response. General Smith's evidence and associated documents also describe a meeting which General Smith attended in Belgrade on 15 July 1995 with, inter alia, Slobodan Milosevic, Ratko Mladic, Carl Bildt, Thorvald Stoltenberg, and Yasushi Akashi and discussions at that meeting about Srebrenica. It was agreed by all the participants that the presence of Ratko Mladic at that meeting in Belgrade would be kept secret. General Smith's evidence explains that the primary purpose of UNPROFOR's mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina during 1995 was to support the delivery of humanitarian aid. When General Smith needed to use armed forces -- armed force to defend UNPROFOR forces in 1995, he would do so. But such actions were taken to protect UNPROFOR units rather than to alter the balance of force or forces in the conflict. Finally, General Smith's evidence describes the centralised command and control system in use by the army of Republika Srpska during 1995. Your Honour, with your permission, there is one passage of General Smith's prior testimony that I would seek to clarify with him. May I do so?

It's like a pecking order, if you like, when looking at a group of people. That's how I meant it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Turning to page 19 quickly. In both, if we could. We have 19 as being a page which has been redacted in its entirety. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could quickly read that page.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Can we move down the page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you like it larger, incidentally?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It's okay. It's only a couple of paragraphs to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Completely up to Mr. Guy-Smith, if it would assist the witness, I have a hard copy, unredacted. No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if that would assist the witness, I'm more than happy for him to have it, if the Chamber deems that to be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have to tell you that since it's my hard copy, there are --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Even if there are interlineations in it, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read what's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can pass it on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. I'm trying to do this as quickly as I can for you, sir. If we can go to -- having read that, do you confirm that's your statement --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That's my statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- and the information contained therein is similarly accurate?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you would say the same again if you were asked the same questions or make the same statement in the -- even in the absence of questions being made?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, page 20. And if you could -- we'll find that 20 suffers a similar fate that 19 suffered, so if we could - meaning that it was entirely redacted - so if we could make a bit bigger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For ease of reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that good, or would you like it bigger?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And could we go down the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And once again, I take it that's your statement which you confirm as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to ask a couple of questions before we go on with the same exercise, which is: If you take a look at the second sentence from the last in the top paragraph which starts with the language: "The meeting was significant because I saw at firsthand Mladic operating as a commander at a strategic level ..."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Could the page be moved, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. You would like it moved up or, I'm sorry, down, I guess yeah.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, I want to see the top. I'll make sure it's moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Okay. This is referring to the meeting that had you with Mladic on the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I just read, and I can't see it now. Which paragraph are you pointing out?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It starts with, "I had a meeting with General" -- one, two, the third paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You got it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm now going to the last two sentences: "The meeting was significant because I saw it firsthand, Mladic operating as a commander at a strategic level playing a central command role to meet the joint HV/HVO offensive." Now, could you explain for us just for the moment because I noticed the word "operating as a commander" -- the phrase "operating as a commander at a strategic level." What does that mean, operating at a commander as a strategic level, militarily? What is the significance of that statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In this case, I had dealt with Mladic on specific issues, entry to Srebrenica or something like that. Here I was actually dealing with him, dealing with a strategic issue in which he was having to consider factors and operate at a higher level to that that I had normally been in contact with him about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If you could be of some help to us, as I understand it, militarily speaking, there are those that operate at strategic level and those that operate at -- I'm sorry, those that function - put it that way - at a strategic level and those that function at an operational level. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. But it doesn't help you much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm looking for help here.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, a senior commander might or might not be dealing with a strategic matter. He is still, if you like, potentially able to deal with a strategic or a large-scale matter. It is -- depending on the circumstances he might find himself dealing with really quite a low-level matter for some reason, perhaps this hasn't -- is deeply interesting to him for another purpose or something like that. So in the case of my relationships with General Mladic, in -- during that year, most of our dealings were over quite specific issues which you might say were of a -- of a local and tactical nature in their detail. However strategic it might have been, in that this was the UNPROFOR commander dealing with the Bosnian Serb army commander. Here, I'm actually witnessing him, engaged with him indeed, over a bigger issue of -- in which he is handling this major offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just also understand, what is this major offensive? Is the operation in Zepa an operational issue or a strategic issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say the Zepa incident was clearly strategic. This was a collapse of an UN Safe Area. The issue -- the actual matters, though, that we were dealing about, prisons exchanges, whether I had access down that road or whatever, are -- are the sort of tactical detail of the day. So on the basis on which our conversations were taking place, were done in the detail. In this case, he -- this offensive is a combined offensive by forces of the -- of Croatia and the Croatian elements of the Federation forces in Bosnia, that is having an impact on the Krajinas in Croatia on Bihac and -- and I can't precisely remember where they are at this stage, but they are certainly threatening, if they are not already on Bosnian territory inside Bosnian borders and are engaged with the Bosnian Serb army. And there's a refugees and so forth, all beginning to flood into the Banja Luka area, and so on. And this -- and we're debating this. This is -- we're not down in the detail. We're dealing with this whole new situation, and I'm seeing him operate at a different level than the detail around a pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just if I might, to make sure that we're clear on our terms. There are -- there's the ability to operate at a strategic level, the ability to function at an operational level, and I believe you introduced a new term here, which is "tactical." And so is there a distinction between those three manners of functioning? I'm going to use the word "function," because obviously if we use "operate" twice, it gets to be confusing. So is there a difference between the function between an operational level and a tactical level? I believe you -- you have explained how to -- what the function is, at a strategic level. I believe you have.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If I could -- at the risk of becoming a school room lecturer, I will try and bring this as simple as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be good.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: At the strategic level, and this is all from a military point of view, at the strategic level, you are translating the political intention into a military action. There clearly has to be a linkage in the two, and you are deciding on such matters as the objectives that are to be achieved, the allocation of forces and resources to achieve those objectives, the priorities of their achievement, et cetera. And trying to achieve a coherent pattern in the whole. I will now leave out the operational level for the moment and go to the tactical.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The tactical is where you actually do the business. If I could take a -- an example, a metaphor for this; consider a building of a major building project. You have an architect and his advisors who translate the vision of the person who wants the building into a plan. He constructs a design. That is in effect the strategic activity. But at some point a man has to come and lay bricks and put windows in and so forth, and those are the tactical activities. Now normally, if it is a small house you don't need anybody in between the two. But as you get a bigger and bigger project, perhaps the building of a major hotel or shopping complex or whatever, now there is a degree of complexity in this, and there are subsidiary decisions that lie between the purely tactical and the strategic. And that is, if you like, the equivalent of the operational level in military affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the metaphor, who would that be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would -- it is normally the theatre commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the metaphor, in the building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the metaphor, oh, it's your protect management team. When you see these big projects, you see a big border up, don't you, with all the different firms, and then there's an even bigger sign on top of it, and that's such-and-such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The architect, project manager, and then builder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a dangerous metaphor because we can go too far down that road, but it ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the strategic level as defined as being putting the political intention into a military level, in this situation - and by "this situation," I mean the one in which you were involved in, for the moment, in July - the political intention would be found in the government of the Republika Srpska, which was headed by Karadzic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In a -- in a -- if you like, in a formal textbook construct, yes, you could probably put it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to that response, you were aware, were you not, that not only was there a president of Republika Srpska but there also was an Assembly that did those things that all assemblies do, which is voting on all matters that affect the republic.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that, too, would be part of the -- for purposes of the model that we're referring to, in terms of what one does at a strategic level that, too, would be a place that a military commander at the strategic level would find his or her - I think it is probable his, for the most part, still in the world - direction, with regard to how to proceed; correct? Not only the president but also the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I mean, how theoretical are we being? If it would help you, I said that the business of strategy for the military point of view is to translate the political intentions into military matters. The general is on that interface. He is a political actor in that sense. And, of course, he knows what is going on in the political sphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, obviously with regard to Mladic that will become an issue that we will discuss at some point today, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now you go to say in the same paragraph: "It exposed Mladic's key position. He had moved to western Bosnia with all of his key advisors and with some special forces we had witnessed him with in Zepa." With regard to this particular sentence, when you refer to his "key advisors," are you -- who are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I can't -- other than I think Gvero was there, General Gvero, I can't remember who else I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I were to mention either Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- I wouldn't be surprised if he was there, either. But I don't remember that -- whether he was in that list of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On this particular --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of those -- of those individuals that you had recognised through your intelligence as being key advisors, could you do us the kindness of telling us who you would identify, in that fashion, who Mladic's key advisors were.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: From memory, Tolimir would have been one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned Gvero?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Gvero, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Those are the only two names that come to mind. I'd have to see a list and -- and refresh my memory considerably to -- to enlarge on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you just one of the names. Does the name Miletic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't immediately recall his position, or as we understood it anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If I were to suggest to you that he was the Chief of Staff, would that be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what about Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Another name. But, again, I would have to refresh my memory as to the relationships of all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And lastly, Colonel Indic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think he would have moved. He was Sarajevo centred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. He was kind of a unique individual, was he not, in terms of military construct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. Why was he unique?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking, because he was someone who had the ear of Mladic and was outside the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He was their liaison officer that we dealt with, and he appeared to have some very direct links to Mladic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean he "was outside the chain of command."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. What I mean by that is he was -- he was able -- he was able to give orders to individuals who had a higher rank than he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that how you understood him, General Rupert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not like that. Do you want to answer again [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Do you want again after your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I understood him to be Mladic's liaison officer based at Lukavica Barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: His business -- he was our point of contact and first point of contact, if you like, with the Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go now down to the next paragraph. So we should probably scroll, I guess, it's down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus on, again, the last two sentences which is, you say: "I shared Mladic's concern at the situation as it was quite clear that fighting would go spread. However, I pointed out that the HV offensive could be justified under Article 51 of the UN Charter?"

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to that, what was the discussion that you had with General Mladic concerning Article 51 being available as a justification for this particular offensive?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I need you to, first of all, get me the Article 51 of the UN Charter. Because I can't remember what it is. Nor do I -- on knowing that might help me to reconstruct what our conversation was about. But I deduce from what is in front of me that he was complaining that the Croatian army was the -- should have been stopped or shouldn't have been there or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Article 51, if all will trust me reads: "Nothing in the Present Charter shall impair the inherent right of individual or collective self-defence if an armed attack occurs against a member of the United Nations until the Security Council has taken measures necessary to maintain international peace and security. Measures taken by members in the exercise of the right of self-defence shall be immediately reported to the Security Council and shall not in any way affect the authority and responsibility of the Security Council under the present Charter to take at any time such action as it deems necessary in order to maintain or restore international peace and security." So I take it from -- from that, that it was your position that the HV offensive was a matter of self-defence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: To be absolute -- to be sure that I am -- that is my position, I would like to understand more of what Mladic and I were talking about. But I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: As to why I had --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why you alluded to Article 51.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm only, as it were, trying to think back to that particular event, and I can't remember what the issue, the particular issue was that led to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. The reason I was asking the question is because you, in this part of your statement, refer to a very specifical - "specifical," I'm doing it all day - specific article of the United Nations charter. So I thought that perhaps you could be of some help to us there.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... fine. Going to the next sentence, you state: "It was interesting to observe that Mladic showed overwhelming concern for the integrity of the Republika Srpska and expressed little interest about the possibility of an HV offensive into the Krajinas." So I take it by this, what was -- what was being discussed in the conversation was what I -- what I'll term what he believed to be the -- the importance of the geographic integrity of the Republika Srpska as he had defined it.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It was more -- I mean, that's how it -- it can be interpreted, I agree. But the -- my memory of that particular point was that much of the rhetoric and discussions about Republika Srpska had in the past included our brother Serbs in the Krajinas. And this -- the presentation was that the -- we were all of one people, we, the Serbs, were all of one people, that we must understand this as an entity. And what I'm referring to there was that when -- now, when the pressure was on, this wasn't so apparent at all and that Mladic is interested only in the boundaries of Republika Srpska, as opposed to the Krajinas, where the Croatian Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And so -- and so we're clear, this conversation, being a conversation, as you termed it, at a strategic level entertains obviously then the political intention of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: As being interpreted by Mladic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to -- if we could go to the next page, which is 21, and take a look at the very first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And go to the very bottom of the page and take a look at the last paragraph. And then we're going to have to go over to the next page to complete that particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the first full sentence in the page that you're looking at: "He also reiterated the Bosnian Serb wish to be involved in the peace process acclaiming that the FRY are distant from this war." Okay?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard -- with regard to that statement, I take that he evidenced some concern that he would not be involved in the peace process, or that other parties were trying to do things that were antithetical to what he believed was appropriate resolution for peace.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall his making any judgement about his motivation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did he say something to the effect that, you know, Gee willikers, we'd want to be part of it too. I mean, how did this come up?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you don't remember, you don't remember. Okay. Once again with regard to those two paragraphs, do you confirm that was your statement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you confirm the information that is contained therein?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it's accurate?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we go to page 23, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I apologise, I made a mistake, 24, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very -- very first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That's the one beginning: "... early October ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If then if we could go back to page 23. I'm sorry, there was a question that I wanted to ask you with regard to that. Which is the paragraph which is -- one, two, three, it's the fourth paragraph, which I believe is paragraph 112. We don't need -- we can work off of the P2348, that's fine. Either way, it makes no deference. It says: "On 10 September, the Force Commander had a second meeting with Mladic, the latter refused to negotiate without a stop to the bombing."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the bombing that is occurring here, could you -- you help us out in terms of which particular bombing was occurring that Mladic was stating he refused to negotiate unless it stopped?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. The -- from -- and we don't need to check the dates, but the very end of August a series of attacks are initiated which include bombing by NATO's 5th Tactical Air Force. There's a pause after about three days, and then it -- it starts again. So this is in the second stage of that, from my memory, and the -- the siege of Sarajevo has been lifted, aid is flowing in at that stage, but bombing is continuing. But at exactly what stage it is reached by the 10th of September, I'm not sure without, looking at a chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of stopping the bombing, when you were meeting with Mladic, did you inform him that you were not in a position to stop the bombing, being a commander of UNPROFOR, and that the issue of the bombing halting was a matter that had to be raised with NATO?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: By that stage, I mean, I'm not at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, I understand that. But do you know if that was a topic of the conversation, that there was division between the UNPROFOR, UNPROFOR authority and the NATO authority? And the reason I'm asking you this question is because, obviously, at some other -- at times the question about the division of authority became -- became an issue. But if you do know, that's great; if you don't know, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that he was not at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The question appears to call for speculation. The gentleman says he was not at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Absolutely. We will take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. If I could, Your Honour, with regard to the document that we were discussing that had been up on the screen, if I could have introduced into evidence, those paragraphs that we were discussing, which were paragraphs 85, 88 to 100, and 104 which had been redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are admitted. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those paragraphs will be Exhibit D96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have said: "War no longer exists." "Confrontation, conflict, and combat undoubtedly exist all around the world," and you have defined a number of places where that occurs. "States still have armed forces which they still use as a symbol of power, nonetheless, war is cognitively known to most non-combatants. War is battle in the field between men and machinery. War is a massive deciding event and a dispute in international affairs. Such war no longer exists." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss with you, obviously, I saw the smile on your face, and I'm sure you know from where that comes, or from whence that comes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do, yes. Opening paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is the opening paragraph in "The Utility of Force: The Art of War in the Modern World," a book that you, yourself, penned, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the events in Bosnia, and specifically concerning what has been called the siege of Sarajevo, would you define that as the classic war that we, as non-combatants, are used to, or is this the new kind of confrontation, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think I understand it. It was the part of the -- it was -- the fighting around Sarajevo, it was part of the conflict within the confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to see if we could get some understanding, because I believe that you have indicated that there are number of specific factors or considerations that one needs to address, I think you've called them major trends, with regard to understanding confrontations and conflicts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And those are the ends for which we are fighting, are changing from the hard absolute objectives of interstate industrial war to more malleable objections to do with the individual and societies that are not states?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We fight amongst -- that's the first. The second is we fight amongst the people. The fact amplified literally and figuratively by the central role of the media. We fight in every living-room in the world, as well as on the streets and fields of a conflict zone? Right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that by this you were alluding to the fact that the media is now being used -- being used in a manner of weaponry by both sides to the conflict that previously we did not see, the propaganda war has become more pervasive in these conflicts?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm not making such a absolutely direct linkage as you described.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I -- remember, I call all six of those factors, of which you have mentioned two, trends, and I don't in any way suggest that they are, you know -- absolutely -- each one is the same in every case, or that are combination is the same in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to this trend, then, being the media trend, as the media trend that you've recognised as being one of the trends that now exists, was used with regard to the conflict in the entirety of the former Yugoslavia, would you agree that the propaganda war that was fought reached new heights in this conflict, as compared to others previously held?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. You are -- you are making a -- when I am talking about the media in that trend of -- of fighting amongst the people, it divides, as you explained, into two packets. There is the physical and literal fighting amongst the people, and then there is the media. And somewhere in that book I explain that the book are what they say they are, a medium, within which you operate. Now, use of propaganda is as old as time. And the -- I wouldn't argue that it was any more or less in this particular case. If you go to the Second World War, you can see it all there too. I don't think you can scale things in the way you are asking me the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to the use of propaganda, would you be in a position to comment as to whether or not propaganda was used more by the Bosnian Presidency, and by that I mean the Muslims' side at an international level, as opposed to the Bosnian Serb side, in terms of a device to fight the war?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Would you define for me what you mean by "propaganda"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Propaganda is a statement which is used to influence a party with regard to a particular event, which may or may not be true.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The event or the -- or the statement isn't true?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The statement may or may not be true.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: So advertising is propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, according to Edward Bernays it most certainly is, yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In which case all parties were doing it in equal measure. I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You can't distinguish or delineate between them. Very well. The third trend you note is that: "Our conflicts tend to be timeless, since we are seeking a condition which then must be maintained until an agreement on a definitive outcome, which may take years or decades." Right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The fourth is: "We fight so as not to lose the force, rather than fighting by using the force at any cost to achieve the aim." Could you expand on that particular trend, please?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The fighting not to lose the force?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm contrasting this with what I called "industrial war," the previous paradigm, in which with conscription with industrialisation we could risk and lose whole armies and create new ones. And you see this happening on a number of occasions during, for example, the Second World War. This allows you to conduct and take quite strategic risks, if you wish to, because the consequence of failure isn't utterly catastrophic because you have the capacity to build a new army. In our current circumstances, and this is the argument in the book, we can no longer take those strategic risks with your force, and so you are conducting your operations on the basis that you cannot risk the totality of the force. It would be strategically catastrophic. That's the essence of the argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The fifth is on each occasion, new uses are found for old weapons. "Those constructed specifically for use in a battlefield against soldiers and heavy armaments now being adapted for our current conflicts, since the tools of industrial war are often irrelevant to war amongst the people." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I think there is a bit more in that quote than just that bit you have read. I'm explaining that it is much about the organisation and so forth of the weapons as the -- as the actual weapon itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, if I might just ask, where are we going with these questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Towards what occurred here in this particular case and what this particular gentleman was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope we get there soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will be there in a moment. Could we please have 1D01-0620 up on the screen. And specifically page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we're on the same page, what I read was -- this particular language here. Which is "on each occasion new uses are --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine. I recognise that, but you're also reading from the opening instruction in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed so.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And there is a bit more about it further down the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And that's all I'm alluding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And the last point being that: "The sides are mostly non-state ..." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't need that any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the conflict that you were involved in for UNPROFOR, you first became aware of the general difficulties that existed, I believe, prior to you being seconded to the area, correct? In 1992, you were working inside the British, I believe, Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I could be mistaken there.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like it just comment on your first statement. I don't think, at least initially, UNPROFOR was involved in the conflict. UNPROFOR was part of the confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Could you -- could you help us there by what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I do not use conflict and confrontation as synonyms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. A confrontation occurs and need not -- when two parties or more parties, but we'll keep it to two, have a different outcome and view.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It -- they don't have to resolve it by conflict. You go to court, you can obey the traffic rules or whatever. If you default, as it were, default to fighting about it, you have a conflict and that is the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Can I expand on that if you want to, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I think I understand what you are saying here, and to the extent it is of assistance, I'm sure we will be talking about a bit -- in a bit. You first receive -- you first became acquainted with the region and the difficulties that were existing while you were still in London working for the Ministry of Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And during that period of time, were you involved in any of the discussions -- well, let me ask you this first: Were there discussions that existed with NATO forces before you went to Bosnia concerning the use of NATO air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, but not with the NATO force. This was my involvement and it was as staff officer in London dealing with the NATO headquarters in Brussels, and, for that matter, with the UN headquarters in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that before you went to Sarajevo there was a division of opinion with regard to the use of air-strikes in the region? And by that I mean, there was an argument over whether or not there should be bombing from the air as a sole mechanism, or whether or not the air-strikes should be supporting ground troops?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, there wasn't an argument in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If it would help you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: You had two organisations in which different groups of states were represented: The United Nations, on the one hand, and NATO on the other. The -- what was on, if you like, and the nations who were -- had forces deployed on the ground were in some cases represented in both political entities, NATO and the UN, and in other -- other cases they were only represented in one or the other. And there was certainly different views in those two groupings which had to be brought together. But it wasn't a question of whether they should be -- it was an either/or between bombing or ground support.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you involved in the discussions concerning this matter in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not in 1992. In 1993 and 1994, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were involved in those discussions in 1993 and 1994, you were involved in your capacity, I take it as a member of the British army and the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, before we go any further for the moment, did you take into consideration when you were negotiating with Mladic, to the extent that you were, that the negotiations were oftentimes for what I will call side benefits or side effects as opposed to having a negotiation for -- for an actual -- actually, what was going on, and by that I mean, if you were negotiating for a cease-fire, you had received information, quite frankly, there were other things afoot. The negotiations were also being used for purposes of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think it is quite a compound question. Perhaps it could be broken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you were negotiating with Mladic for certain specific events to occur, did you take into consideration the fact that those negotiations were actually being used as part of the war; that Mladic was not there to negotiate with you necessarily in good faith but, rather, for purposes of obtaining some other benefit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I don't comprehend your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUT-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll retreat from the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, counsel is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object again to the use of the term "the fact" in Mr. Guy-Smith' question, because I don't think there's been any establishment of -- certainly during this cross-examination of any such facts that he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In addition to that, Mr. Guy-Smith, I would like to say I'm not quite sure whether you want Mr. Smith to be able to tell you what went on in the mind of Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, that I don't want him to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but then when you say that Mladic was negotiating, with a view to other benefits, how is he supposed to know unless Mladic told him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will go at it another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you went to the region, would be characterize your mandate as being that one of peacekeeping?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't think it -- there was no -- the peace wasn't there. There was a Cessation of Hostilities Agreement when I arrived but no more. My mandate was essentially to protect and -- and ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since, as you put it, "there was a Cessation of Hostilities Agreement and no more," what did you understand the rules of engagement to be with regard to your presence there? What could you do; what couldn't you do?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: What did I understand the rules of engagement to be with regard to -- well, the rules of engagement were given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And, again, essentially, the rules of engagement were wholly reactive. We -- we, the UN, initiated nothing, in terms of the use of force. You were reacting to a situation in which force was being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if force was being used, then, with regard to the rules of engagement, you could respond in self-defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The individuals in that situation, yes, could.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the notion of an air-strike, the air-strikes were not within the rules of engagement, were they?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not in the documentation, if you like, that was being issued to the -- the commanders on the ground and their -- their subordinates. In terms at the level I had, there were, in effect, rules of engagement, which was a series of agreed documents as to how and in what circumstances air-strikes could be called in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the rules of engagement that you're referring to as to how and in what circumstances air-strikes would be called in, were those agreements within the function of the mandate of peacekeeping?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: There isn't a mandate of peacekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Were those documents within the mandate that you had?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To engage in air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't -- again, I'm finding this difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll put it in other terms for you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The -- go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you find it difficult to follow, I will put it in other terms for you. When a decision was made for an air-strike to occur --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- where did you find the authority to do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whose strike? UNPROFOR strike -- have air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, UNPROFOR air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is whether UNPROFOR air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay [Overlapping speakers] ... I'll answer -- I'll take care of your concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were there UNPROFOR air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR commander or his superiors could request an air-strike. The air-strike would have been carried out by the force found from NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When the UNPROFOR commander or his superiors requested an air-strike, what were the criteria used for that request to be made?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- would -- to be absolutely precise, I would need to look at a whole range of documents which start with the United Nations Resolutions and so forth that came out in the period during 1993 and 1994, covering these circumstances. But on the basis of my memory, there were two reasons, if you like, for calling in an air-strike. The first was in close air support in self-defence of -- sorry. The first was for close air support in air -- in self-defence of a unit or UN -- an element of the UNPROFOR on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the second?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And the second was to enforce the exclusion zones around -- I'm sorry, the exclusion zones which I need to backtrack a bit. There are things called safe areas, and over time these developed into the idea of exclusion zones, which inside an exclusion zone, the heavy weapons were either supposed not to be there or held in what were called Weapon Collection Points. And as a means and air power was available to be called for to enforce those exclusion zones, and I have to be reminded of the date when they started, but it was sometime in 1994, if I recall correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to air power being called in to enforce the exclusion zones, I take it that when there was a violation of the exclusion zone by either side that UNPROFOR would first seek in its capacity to remedy the situation by having whatever was violative of the exclusion zone brought back into the -- the proper form. And by that I mean, as I understand -- as I understand it, there were, for example, certain areas where heavy weapons were not supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. And you didn't necessarily -- the idea did not -- you were not expected to use air power as the first action, if a heavy weapon appeared in an exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: You were expected to deal with the matter in a graduated way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say, "you were expected to deal with the matter in a graduated way," by that you were referring to UNPROFOR was expected to deal with that in a graduated way. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And did the graduated way that UNPROFOR was expected to deal with that include the threat of air-strikes if there was not compliance?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, yes. That had been there since the -- that threat, that prospect had been there from the outset of the establishment of those exclusion zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your memory, was there ever a threat made to the BiH with regard to violation of the exclusion zone by UNPROFOR? And by the threat, being the threat of an air-strike?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: UNPROFOR can't -- couldn't violate an exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, BiH, the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: But -- I thought you had said that it was -- a threat it was -- UNPROFOR had violated the exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, there should have been a comma there. To your memory, was there ever a threat by UNPROFOR to the BiH?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked not to speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please don't speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the exclusion zones, when they were established and authorised by the Security Council and so forth, contained in that authorisation the -- the threat, if we like to call it that, that the NATO air power could to be used to enforce them. It was to -- it was -- the exclusion zones applied to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Part of what -- I'm trying to understand here is the function of UNPROFOR. We have heard testimony that UNPROFOR's role was that of a peacekeeper, which you have rejected. So I'm trying to get a sense of how you would characterize UNPROFOR's presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least at the time that you were there.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I rejected the title of peacekeeper on what you might think rather narrow grounds, that there wasn't a peace to keep. And much of the concept of being a peacekeeper, particularly at the time and in the United Nations, was that you were, as it were, standing between two people who were agreed, given your presentation, to remain at peace. Perhaps an example would be Cyprus and the UN deployment there for some decades.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That certainly wasn't the case that you were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Exactly. And that is why I said we weren't peacekeepers. However, there is a very large number of people at the time in particular who understood what we were doing and why they had sent us there and so forth, to be more in that example, that spirit, if you like, that you're not involved in the fighting as such. You're there to assist and ameliorate the condition of refugees and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand what you said, and perhaps you can be of some assistance here, and this may be because I'm naive, but I've heard there is a distinction between being a peacekeeper and being a peacemaker. And by that I mean, when one has the mandate of being a peacemaker, then they can engage in active behaviours, such as offensives or bombings in order to achieve an objective which is distinct from that of being a peacekeeper.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'd -- you may not -- I don't want to connect, I don't agree with your direct connection of offensives or bombings and being a peacemaker. Those are not necessarily a connection to be made there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you see a distinction between the function of peacekeeping and peacemaking?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Clearly, if you have made -- if you had been party to making a peace, then you might, indeed, find yourself being party to keeping it, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to making the peace, what different activities would exist, if any, in your mind? And I'm speaking militarily.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If -- if you -- if a political entity wishes to use its military to create a condition of peace, then it can be done. But in doing that, you have to decide what it is you want your military to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: To that end.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to UNPROFOR's presence was - in your mind -- in your mind in understanding - the United Nations's wish that the military be used to create a condition of peace, as you have just stated?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. Our military actions were all couched in the understanding that they were there for self-defence, and then a bit later on, defence increasing defence, if you like, of refugees and so forth within the Safe Areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was the function of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The function of NATO was somewhat distinct? And that's a question. In your -- in your understanding --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I was distinct, in fact, in that it wasn't on the ground; it was in the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from it not being on the ground and in the air, NATO was not in the same situation that UNPROFOR was in, and by that I mean NATO had the ability to bomb in the absence of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is it your position that the bombings that NATO engaged in in 1994 and 1995 were self-defensive?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not of NATO. But that's why they were there. Either in -- being used in -- in -- within the self-defence of the UN force; or, subsequently, in the exclusion zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the exclusion zones those bombs certainly were self-defence, were they?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, the defence of the amelioration of the situation in the Safe Areas, you begin to see developing during that time the use of air power, use of force, in supporting that idea of the exclusion zones. And then it then develops further in -- during 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And clearly what we're discussing here is information that was communicated to both armies, and by that I mean to the Bosnian Serb army as well as to the BiH?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- these things were publicised and so forth, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You made a determination relatively earlier on in your tenure that neither side was interested in maintaining what you have termed the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think I would call it -- that was my view. Whether it was a determination, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I will -- we'll use your term, then, which is "view." And if I'm not mistaken, you determined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You viewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to say "you determined," Your Honour, and I will tell you why.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You determined, and I'm now referring to your statement, paragraph 34 that at the end of this series of meetings referring to meetings that you had with General Mladic, "I had come to the conclusion that the Bosnian Serbs had concluded that further fighting was inevitable."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just to assist the witness, can we at least let him know what dates we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This would be March 7th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And could we give him the statement. Let him look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. That's P2348. And could we go to -- I believe it's page 9, paragraph 34.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. And I'm referring to the following language of yours. "At the end of this series of meetings, I had come to the conclusion that the Bosnian Serbs had concluded that further fighting was inevitable and they had to reach some form of conclusion within the year."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is when, I believe, you formed what you have called your thesis; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you describe for the Chamber what your thesis was.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, it was a thesis. This was a basis on which I was working. It wasn't necessarily, you know, what was going to happen or anything like. This was my understanding of a situation where I couldn't see everyone's cards. The -- and it was essentially, as has already been said, that the balance of forces and so on was such that this -- that both parties would be seeking a conclusion during this year, if they could possibly arrive at one. And that the eastern enclaves, which, from the Bosnian Serb point of view, were in their rear, were absorbing a -- a proportion of their manpower that they could more usefully use elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we just stop there for a moment. When you say that -- "from the Bosnian Serb point of view," in your thesis, had you analysed the respective manpower that was available to the Bosnian Serbs and to the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that was what I meant when I said in the balance of forces and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And what -- what was the -- your analysis in that regard and your findings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that the Bosnian Serbs had more space to defend than they had people to defend it, in essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you indicate in the same paragraph that the UN were being used as shields by the Bosnians and hostage by the Serbs. And I believe -- this is another one of ideas that you came up with, with regard to the presence of UNPROFOR in the area, which is the hostage shield dilemma?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Again, this is -- at the time was centred on the eastern enclaves, where the -- UNPROFOR's presence in the enclave allowed -- acted, to some extent, as a shield for the defenders, the Bosnian forces on the inside. On the other hand, we, the UN, were also in the enclave, and, therefore, getting to those people. Supporting those people, our UN people, and to carry out our mandate of getting the aid and so forth into those enclaves, we were hostage to the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the first matter that you mentioned which is that you were -- you, the UN, were present in the enclaves, as were members of the BiH, could you tell us, with regard to your delivery of aid how you distinguished the aid that you were giving to non-military -- as opposed to military purposes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: You need to ask the UNHCR who were the people who were distributing the aid or Medicins Sans Frontieres or whomsoever. My business was to get it there and to -- and to deliver it and see it was delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard -- with regard to your purpose, you understood, of course, that by getting it there, the UNPROFOR forces would be necessarily perceived as taking one side, no matter what the protestations were, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we're talking -- first of all, we're talking about -- first of all, the question is unclear, necessarily perceived by whom? Second of all, if we're talking about, again, people's perceptions, we appear to be talking about speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As you told us, your purpose was to get aid to the enclave; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The aid that you got to the enclave included foodstuffs, fuel; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Medicine; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Those would -- I mean, there was blankets and things, no doubt. I would be -- you know, we would have to go and look at the lists and manifests.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. With regard to the aid that was being supplied, at the time the aid was being supplied, you, in your capacity as an UNPROFOR commander, were aware of the fact that there were soldiers in the enclave; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Bosnian soldiers or UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Bosnian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm assuming -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any protests concerning the delivery of aid to an enclave where there were Bosnian soldiers from the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever receive delivery of aid ... I'm confused by the question. There were not Bosnian Serb forces in an enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. My question is, did you receive any protests from the Bosnian Serb forces with regard to the delivery of aid where there were Bosnian soldiers who were members of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: On the few occasions that we got aid in, there were -- there was at least one that I can recall of a complaint, that -- and I can't remember the specific -- but there was definitely a complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the complaint revolved around the issue that you were aiding one of the factions, excuse me, strike that word. One of the armies to the conflict. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If I recall the complaint it was a great deal more specific than that. It was that there were things that shouldn't be there, in -- in the -- hidden in one of the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What kind of things would that be?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It was weapons or ammunition. I can't remember the particular detail. But I can remember that there was such an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it went beyond the issue of just the delivery of aid.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed. This was a specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In which -- in which there was a complaint that UNPROFOR assets had been used to deliver weapons and munitions to --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: There --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Bosnian army members?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. They had been found. It was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who stopped it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb inspection. As they came in, they found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. That must -- that must have diminished your credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection. Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, it calls for speculation. Credibility in the eyes of whom, from whom? We don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was it of concern to you that an UNPROFOR -- I'm going use the word "convoy," and that could be too much. But was it of concern to you that an UNPROFOR asset was stopped and weapons and munitions were found by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it was of concern. And it -- it wasn't an UNPROFOR asset. I'd go back and tell you, we were there to guard the convoys, see them getting in. We didn't load the trucks or anything like that. Nevertheless, thereafter, I made sure that there was a great deal more attention paid to what went on the trucks and how they were managed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who -- who was providing this aid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The primary agency was the UNHCR, who -- who organised the actual deliveries and what went on the trucks and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this consignment in which weapons were found was destined for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. My memory of the incident is in the fairly early stages of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to turn to paragraph 40 of your statement and just have you confirm, I think, what you may have -- you may have already briefly said, which is that you took the view, which is different than coming to a conclusion, as you had done with the Bosnian Serbs that the Bosnian government had no intention of extending the COHA, that's the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, beyond the end of April. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With that in mind, did that change the nature of what you felt you were going to be able to do on the ground, where both parties clearly were moving towards a -- breaking the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it was -- fighting was already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It certainly -- the situation had certainly changed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, with regard to paragraph 43. This is in terms of you having a meeting with Dr. Karadzic; that would be the president of the Republika Srpska. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you were meeting with Karadzic because Mladic refused to meet with you, right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He wasn't an alternative. It is true that Mladic was refusing to meet with me and Karadzic was, so I met with him. But they weren't alternatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, well, by virtue of the fact that Mladic refused to meet with you was why you went to meet with Karadzic, correct, you contacted Karadzic? Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. But that -- it isn't -- you're making it sound as though they were alternatives. I was meeting with the head of the Bosnian Serb and would have done so anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were meeting with the head of the Bosnian Serb what, sir?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs. He was their president.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And why had you -- had your communication with General Mladic ceased, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Amongst other reasons of which I'm not aware, because the one that he was telling me about, was that I had rejected two of his liaison officers from a headquarters in -- in fact the British headquarters in Sector Sarajevo -- not Sector Sarajevo, Sector South-west and sent them back to his headquarters in -- at some point about two weeks before that, I think, if I remember the timing correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to your meeting with Karadzic, Karadzic informed you that we will counterattack where we have been attacked. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If I have written it yes, then, I write that there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you put that in quotes as something that he said.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Then -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that statement made in reference to attacks by NATO, attacks by the UN, attacks by the BiH, do you know? Can you help us out there?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I think it is the BiH. And the UN hadn't carried out any attacks at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 44 there was a discussion with regard -- between you and Dr. Karadzic with regard to attacks by NATO; correct? Or so you relate. "He claimed that the BiH were attacking from Srebrenica on a regular basis, and the BSA had taken casualties. Karadzic expressed no concern about the threat of NATO and announced a clear preparedness to take NATO on."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
