utterances.text: Okay. Did he expand at all on that and how that was going to occur? Did he tell you what his plans were, his thinking was in that regard?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, other than I reported in that paragraph, 44, I don't think he did that I can remember anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And paragraph 45 you indicate that: "This comment and his general tone made it quite clear that Karadzic was exercising a high degree of political control and was effectively in charge of the Bosnian Serb strategy and policy at this stage."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That was my impression, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You go on to say, "there was some speculation at the time there was a rift between Karadzic and Mladic." And when you say that there was some speculation, was that speculation on your part, or was that speculation in the international community, was there discussions about that? Can you please expand on that.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I -- I don't really remember how wide the discussion was. Can I certainly remember that we were trying to understand, or I was trying to understand with my immediate staff what the relationship was. So -- but how wide that speculation existed, I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Within the context of your experience with General Mladic, would it be fair to say that, based upon your experience with him in the times that you met with him, that he indicated no interest in political aspirations but confined himself to those of a military sort?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I -- no, I don't think I see it quite like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How do you see it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: As I explained earlier, he was in that position where policy is and the political factors are translated into the military. You cannot detach yourself if you are to do that job from the political. Your emphasise your weight, if you like, lies in the military, but you are joined in the political process, or you can't translate the political activity into military effect. And the -- and I think I cover that in effect when I say in that paragraph 45: "My assessment, with the benefit of hindsight, is that ..." At the time his weight lay in preparing for the offensive. That doesn't mean to say that he was detached from the political process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. My point, and clearly we're not connecting, my point is that you did not -- you did not in your experience with Mladic find that he had political aspirations, did you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I -- no. He never once mentioned that he wanted to be the president, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You have seen what's in my mind. And, as a matter of fact, he made it very clear that he was following the political agenda of his president, Dr. Karadzic, in your meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't recall him saying it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps the language I'm using is inexact. But would it be fair to say that you understood that was his intent?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, that calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you help us at all with the language --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're rephrasing?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you help us at all with any of the language that General Mladic used that brought you to the conclusion that he was not interested in being the president?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: What I said was that I don't recall him saying that that's what he wanted to be. I -- I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it's the absence of this statement.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. In terms of the thesis that you had developed in March concerning the COHA and the consequences that would flow from that, I take it that you engaged in an analysis with regard to what would be the consequences of the conflict starting up in the various enclaves; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. And you are -- you're making more of a thesis than I -- than I was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Did you take into consideration what the consequences would be when the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement was no longer operative with regard to the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I think the question has just been asked an answered, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I have asked a different question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where was it asked and answered, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The question -- the previous question, 8 to 12. And then the answer beginning at 13. Appears to me to be the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's not the same question. One deals with the thesis, and the other deals with whether he took something into consideration. Since he corrected me and said that I made more of his thesis than there was, I'm asking a question to make a determination of what -- whether or not he took this particular issue into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The concern I have, Your Honour, is what the difference between engaging in an analysis regarding an event and taking into consideration consequences of the same event?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, a thesis has within it, a conclusion; whereas an analysis has within it a series of factors that may reach a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could ask the second question again, because I've lost it somewhere on this screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you take into consideration what the consequences would be when the Cessation of Hostilities Agreement was no longer operative with regard to the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was the sort of things I was thinking about was going to -- difficulty of getting the convoys in. In fact, that was already proving difficult. The -- and generally maintaining my ability to carry out my mandate of getting the aid and so forth into those enclaves. That is what I was thinking about then, as I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I want to move to the incident at Markale II for some time. With regard to Markale II, at the outset there was a question with regard to who was responsible for the bombing; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, we had to carry out an investigation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the investigation that was carried out, there were, would it be fair to say, a number of different views as to who was responsible? And let me explain to you what I mean by that. You, I believe, during the time of the investigation, got a hold of General Mladic concerning this particular event; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You asked that General Mladic investigate as to whether or not VRS forces were involved in the shelling that resulted in the Markale II incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think I did that. But I -- I can't recall exactly what I asked of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: You may have a record there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have a record. I'm going read you something and see whether or not that refreshes your recollection as to whether or not you asked General Mladic to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the document that I'm referring to is R0662224 previously tendered exhibits, and I'm referring to page 25. "At 1413 hours on the 28th August, General Smith spoke on the telephone to General Mladic for ten minutes concerning the shelling of Sarajevo that morning. Mladic informed General Smith that he been briefed on the incident only five minutes before the call. General Smith informed him of the circumstances of the shelling and the fact that an excess of 30 people had been killed and more than 40 wounded. "General Smith explained the seriousness of the incident, and his surprise in light of our discussions last week on the process --" excuse me, "on the progress of the peace process, General Smith informed me that the shelling was in clear breach of the NATO ultimatum. Mladic stated that his staff had confirmed that no fire orders had been issued to his units. He agreed to check that no weapons had been fired without authority." Does that refresh your recollection as to whether or not had you a conversation with Mladic --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Concerning -- concerning --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would this be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This would be convenient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you so much. And if we could go down to the third entry, which is 291000, August 1995.

Without going into the issue of whether or not it had been orchestrated by the BiH or not, with regard to the -- the urging by Mladic that a joint commission be set up to engage in the investigation, to your knowledge, was this done?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, there wasn't a joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Was there, to your knowledge, ever a request by UNPROFOR to involve any FRY officials in an investigation of the Markale incident?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the things that did occur --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could have -- I'm done with that exhibit now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before it gets off the screen, General Smith, what would the number 291000 August 1995, how is that deciphered? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could we now have P2356 up on the screen. I'm sorry, because I have a face page for this document which is not a part of -- of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to -- I'm going to read you something, and then I will have to ask that there be a bar table submission. It's the page that I have, which is the front page of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean a bar table submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I have to discuss the matter, I think, first of all, with Mr. Saxon. I have a face page which is a code cable page which is from HQ UNPROFOR Sarajevo office of Lieutenant-General Rupert Smith, and it's a form which there's -- then attached the document that is here but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to put that on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then we can all see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, what do we have to do? Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down a little bit. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I want to refer to the second paragraph which is: "We wish to repeat our views and concerns raised" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt, but I think there is some confusion here. This page that we're looking at here, you see up at the top left-hand corner, it's dated the 8th of September. And it's my understanding that what we were looking at a moment ago, P2356 is dealt with separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. That was the way it was sent to me. I'm happy -- if it's P67, then I'm happy to have it as P67. It's already in evidence. I have no reason to reinvent the wheel here. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just before we remove this one, once again, General, I see now you have added a B. If you look at that top left corner -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The time has got a B now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those have got -- that's the time zone you're in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's this globalized world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. P67, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the second paragraph, it says: "We wish to repeat our views and concerns raised in our fax of 021925Z, September." So what would that be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 2nd of September -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... we are entering a mine field here of procedure. One of the reasons you have this system is it goes on all the signals and messages being sent, and it doesn't matter where they are sent from anywhere in the world, you can work out in what order they came. And the -- say you have the date, time, and the time has the letter after it, if it's -- you need to. And if you're working between New York and Sarajevo, then you need to know in what time zone signals were sent, messages were sent. And Zulu is Greenwich mean time. And you count two hours before Zulu is Bravo, all the way around the world, until you come back to Z again. And then -- and that's why that's there. And so a capable that was coming from New York or we were sending to New York would most certainly have the time zone in its title in order to be clear when the thing was originating.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. "That this report should be treated with the considerable care and discretion. We must continue to be cautious about revealing our evidence and data to public scrutiny?" Could you tell me what is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it's covered later on. We've got nothing to hide, but by -- we don't want to enter into the debate that was going on at the time of, he did it; no, he didn't; he did it, type of argument that was part of the -- the speculation, if you like, that was going on around us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. So when you're saying: "But by declaring our information, we risk entering an expert argument which led a judgement. Other so-called experts have been or continue to be selective in what evidence they chose to consider and adduce to support their judgements." Now with regard to the debate that was going on at that time, I take it that the debate was who was responsible for the Markale incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in order to get to the bottom of this debate, the objective scientific, if that is a proper term. Let me rephrase that. The objective information that was available was not necessarily in the hands of all of the individuals who were part of this debate; is that correct? For example --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He did it, no; he didn't do it, type of argument that was going on, was certainly not informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But here you have this issue of other so-called experts. So with regard to -- with regard to the issue of expertise, there were other individuals who were weighing in with regard to who was responsible, based upon an analysis of what evidence they had; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I can't recall the substance of the debate or who all the other, you know, people were. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But do you recall a Russian colonel by the name of Demurenko?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And he weighed in on who was responsible with regard to this incident, did he not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: He was involved in -- and again, I would have to see the chronology of when who said what, but he was certainly involved at one stage. I think, if I recall correctly, his fears or opinions changed. But I can't -- I don't recall in what order everybody was talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I right that we're speculating here? The one possibility is also that they might have had the same evidence, and it is question of interpretation of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to get to, and I will in a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is -- but for a moment, since we have taken a slight digression, and I apologise, Demurenko was a Russian who was a member of UNPROFOR; correct.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Demurenko made a public statement with regard to the issue of the Markale incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In which he --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, put it this way. I think his statement became public.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Whether he made a public statement, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And his public statement -- the statement that was made that became public was a statement that attributed responsibility to some party other than the Bosnian Serb army; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not sure that was what he said, no. I -- I don't think he was as definite as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So, as you sit here today, you recall him being in a conjectural mode, perhaps, as to who --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- was responsible --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- and had not come up with a definitive view?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall a definitive view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was the information that is contained in this report --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The report that is in front of us.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The report that is covered by this --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that information revealed to General Mladic, to your knowledge? Was he sent a copy of this report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. I don't think he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was any member of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that the speakers do not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was any member --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was any member of the FRY government, to your knowledge, supplied with this report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I -- not by my headquarters anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And specifically do you know whether or not General Perisic was supplied with this report?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to complete the circle, do you know whether any BiH authorities were copied with this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not by my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was, indeed, my next question, Your Honour. I was going to get them all in there.

utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.text: Thank you. I am done with that exhibit. And it has already been introduced into evidence, so we don't need to do anything further with it. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to you take a -- a look -- at this -- at this map and see, first of all, by looking at it if you can familiarize yourself with the area at all.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think I'm looking at Sarajevo. Can we bring it up a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we can, yes.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: But I can't read ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No good showing me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If we could try to expand. There we go. And once again. And once again. And if we could scroll down. And scroll down some more. Up. Stop right there. If we can expand in bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at that, do you recognise the area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You'll note that there are a number of different markings that are on this particular map. And my question to you is: Do you recognise the area of those markings as being areas that were under the control of the BiH?

utterances.text: Well, you've got to be a bit more specific. What markings are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to for example where it says 111 vbbr.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Uh-huh. But not where it says 1 Smbr at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, and that too. I'm just dealing --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Then, no, I don't recognise that as being areas --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise 111 vbbr as being an area that was under the control of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you the same question for 112, 102, 101, 155, 105, and 152 and 115.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the designation 1 smbr, that's not an area that, in your estimation, was under the control of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could pull -- make it smaller. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You will notice there are a couple of markings above where we were before. And do you recognise those areas as being areas that were under the control of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which markings, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 3 Spbr.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that wasn't ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you will notice that there is a dotted line that seems to cover all of the areas that you do recognise as being under the control of the BiH. Would you recognise that as being the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, can I see two. And, yes, I -- there's a red one or a browny one and a blue one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: They more or less mark, as my memory had it, that that was the confrontation line, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, take us along, gentlemen. General Rupert, you said you can see two, and you can see one -- what are you -- what are those -- where's the two, and where is the one?

utterances.text: There's two lines, the dotted lines that surround Sarajevo, there's one in blue and another in either red or brown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Oh, you're not looking at the straight line, solid straight line. Okay.

utterances.text: No, it's the dotted line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The dotted lines, okay. Then I'm with you. Now, what -- what is the -- the question that you were asking, Mr. Guy-Smith was [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Whether he recognises those as being the confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The dotted lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, the dotted lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And that the BiH forces were inside those dotted lines? Is that what you asked a little earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what I'm getting to, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, because I thought you were referring to the solid line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question that was asked by His Honour is the question that I was going ask you, which is within the blue dotted line, that would be the area that's under control of the BiH; correct? And that would be the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the -- the brown dotted line, that would be the area that was the confrontation line where the Bosnian Serb army would be in control.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: On the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: On the outside?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have that moved as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One other question. With regard to this particular map, as you look at it, do you recognise any of the areas that are within the Bosnian-Herzegovina army's control as being points where they had a mortar position?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that exhibit at this time. Perhaps I'm not done; I'm being signalled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have been -- I have asked by my colleague to translate for you the following, which is if we look at the upper left-hand corner of the map --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I need it to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So do I. It's coming up. There are some dates you will notice, where it says -- I'll have Mr. Lukic read it in B/C/S, and it can be translated appropriately, because otherwise I will make a mess of the language. With the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I read this and the interpreters will then interpreter it for the record. So in the upper left-hand corner, it says working map of the Chief of Staff. And then it says in the next line, command of the 12th dKoV. And then the next line says start, 01.03.1995. There are dots dividing the numbers, so I assume this is the date. And then it says completion, the 16th -- or, rather, 16.15. And then it says 14th of September, 1995. And in the right hand corner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Lukic just hold on. Just hold on. Can we go back. We were not told what dKoV stands for. What does that stand for? And Pocetak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you my interpretation. That would be the 12th Division of the ground forces, but I don't want to be the one giving you this interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... interpret Pocetak for us, please, and Zavrsetak. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. But those figures following those words mean a little less to me, unless I know what those words mean. Can the interpreters help, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you want me to translate for you what it says here in the right-hand corner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the defence of the republic. It's in the upper right-hand corner; that's what it says. And then it says military secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Can we scroll to the right, please. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it says in capital letters the defence of the republic. And then underneath it, military secret. And then, strictly confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the lower right-hand corner of this map, right at the bottom of this map, if we can scroll down a little bit, it says Chief of Staff; and then underneath it, colonel; and then underneath it, Rizvo Pleh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which means? Rizvo Pleh?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it's this man's name, since the beginning of both words are capitalised. So I assume it's the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Mr. Guy-Smith. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfectly fine, Your Honour. Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I want to go back and revisit something with you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have P2366 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I shall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could have -- I believe it's page 3 up on the screen, which would be paragraph numbered 12. I'm missing ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We were talking earlier about the issue of fuel. And paragraph 12 of this document, I think, speaks to some of that discussion, which is that: "Over dinner, Mr. Akashi," and that would be yourself, I'm sure sir, "General Smith, and General Janvier protested the denial of fuel convoys to the eastern enclaves. The Bosnian Serbs persisted with the line that UNPROFOR was providing supplies and fuel to the BiH. Of note, Karadzic was heard to remark 'we regard humanitarian and UNPROFOR convoys ... as commercial convoys for the benefit of the Muslims. We are under double restrictions (sanctions), you can expect more restriction.'" With regard to the issue of -- of Karadzic's making this statement, that "the UNPROFOR and humanitarian convoys were commercial convoys for the benefit of the Muslims," can you expand at all in terms of the conversation that was had about these supplies being used for the BiH army? Can you take this any further with regard to what was being said by Karadzic at that time?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon. Mr. Saxon is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The problem with that question is that this paragraph does not mention the BiH army. Is Mr. Guy-Smith suggesting that that is what Mr. Karadzic was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's -- was Mr. Karadzic referring to the BiH army when he was talking about providing supplies and fuel to the BiH?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I don't recall. The -- certainly it can be said we were providing it to those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you were providing it to those enclaves, you're referring to those enclaves where there were BiH army personnel.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: There were -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The army personnel there were such individuals as Commander Delic; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In one of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And Commander Oric?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The name rings a bell again, but I would have to refresh my memory as to where. But, yes, there were commanders and defenders there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And do you by any chance have -- at the time, I'm not asking right now because obviously time has gone by. Did you at the time have intelligence with regard to the strength of those forces in those enclaves where the name Delic was, and perhaps Oric?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Intelligence would be too precise a word.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's a military word. Information.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: We had information largely from our own observations of what was in those -- what the number of defenders and so forth in those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit now. And if we could have now P2360 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a document that refers to a telephone conversation between yourself and General Mladic on the 28th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like to start with page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Page 1, paragraph 1, it states that: "Mladic" -- it says "he claims," so I'm putting Mladic's name in there. "Mladic claimed General Smith was acting on the political direction of the Bosnian government. Mladic demanded the immediate cessation of all NATO combat and transport flights and the unconditional release of detained Serb personnel by 1800 hours that evening." Okay, first of all, do you recall Mladic accusing you of working for the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific incident, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, with regard to the information that's contained in this particular document, was this -- was this information made at or near the time of the conversation that you had with Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm -- I would be confident that this is a good report, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So I take it you can't take us any further with regard to how the conversation progressed with regard to the accusation made by Mladic that you were working for the Bosnian government on May 28th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I can't. Unless there is in a subsequent paragraph this matter is addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to go to paragraph number 4, which is on the next page. And obviously there's a great deal of -- of concern at the time by, I think, both Mladic as well as yourself, with regard to a situation getting heated up that could potentially jeopardize the lives of a number of individuals. But with regard to that, in paragraph 4 it says: "Mladic accept the General Smith's offer to calm the situation and advised him to take a tranquilliser in order to be fit to make reasonable designations." And I take it that was you telling Mladic that he needed to calm down, or is this --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. This is Mladic telling me to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And stop bombing and doing unreasonable things.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, with regard to -- with regard to you calming down, if you could kindly tell us how Mladic was perceiving that you were bombing, since, as I understand it, you were not and NATO was. How did this come about that Mladic was accusing you of these bombings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, because I had made it quite plain to Mladic and in a public statement that if the weapons that had been removed by the Bosnian Serbs from the weapon control points were not put back, then I'd request that sanction be conducted by NATO. And they didn't go back, so I turned my key for the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you turned your key, I -- I understand that there was a double key system between UNPROFOR and NATO, and both keys had to be turned in order for the bombing to commence; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, was your turning of the key, in the subsequent bombing successful?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: We didn't get the weapons back, and I had some -- and I cannot remember the precise number, but it was in the order of 400 people taken hostage eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the question referred to whether the key did turn, and if he says it was not successful, it means that the bombing didn't take place at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's clear it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's clear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Keys were turned. The bombing was ordered, right?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Keys were turned --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should not have used the word "turned the key." I requested NATO to carry out that action. NATO agreed to do so, and it was carried out. It was not successful for the purpose that I had intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the purpose that you had intended it for was to get the heavy weapons back --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: In the exclusion zone -- sorry, into the weapon collection zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Into the weapon collection point?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Of that exclusion zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the bombing that occurred, where did that bombing occur, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it occurred in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to casualties, were there casualties in Pale as a result of that bombing?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I do not recall the extent of the casualties, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I take it by you saying you don't recall the extent of the casualties, there were casualties, it's just that --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I can't say how many or what they were or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right, fine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But casualties, there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then the response to the bombing was that hostages were taken.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Amongst other things, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll just deal with the hostages here for the moment.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the purpose for which you were there, as I understand it, this act, would it be fair to say escalated the problem - and by that I mean the bombing - escalated the problem that existed between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serb army, didn't it? The result of the 400 hostages being taken, it would be the escalation --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It certainly exacerbated it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, exacerbated. So would be it fair to say --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The point I'm making is the problem remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So you were not --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... It got worse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Worse [Overlapping speakers] ... It just made it worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So you were in not in a position where there was, at the time, shall we say, a fair dialogue going on as between you and General Mladic concerning lowering the heat.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm trying to get at is, you had a purpose. Your purpose was to get the weapons back.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You bombed, and you ended up having a bunch of hostages taken?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So you and Mladic were not taking to each other in any particularly effective way in terms of having a peace on the ground, in terms of diminishing anything. And from the standpoint of -- armed conflicts?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: With the hostages being taken, and then the orders I was given as a result of that, there wasn't any conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There wasn't any conflict?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not at that point, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Conflict -- we'll talk about that in a second. Going back to paragraph 4. Mladic says: "If you continue to exercise such unreasonable behavior, he was sure there would be many in the UN who would find themselves in a difficult and finally inextricable situation. He required all NATO flights be stopped. He meant by all this all combat and transport flights as the latter were used to move ammunition and other supplies to the Muslims." That's what he told you; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to that, now, would it be fair to say, if you're looking at it objectively, you are in open hostility with the Bosnian Serb army. You're bombing, they're taking hostages, and he is accusing of supplying the Bosnian-Herzegovinian army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Let's go back to what I said to you about confrontation and convict. No, we have stopped conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: And the confrontation is most certainly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see, and the confrontation being the bombing and the taking of hostages?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, the bombing is conflictual. It didn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the time --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... we remain in a confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the taking of hostages, that is --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That is it part of the confrontation. The taking of them is clearly a conflictual act. But we're now in situation where we are not fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I have been told by my own political authorities to stop. I am not allowed to, as it were, go on bombing and. I'm not allowed to go and - not that I could at the time - as it were, capture my -- recapture the hostages. We are in a different situation, and I don't disagree that we're in confrontation over these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The situation is tense, but there is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Tense, but no blood flowing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No blood flowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to go to paragraph 6 of the same document, where it says: "Mladic asked whether the UN troops were a peacekeeping or an occupying force."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did the conversation go any further than that, or was that just the bold statement that was made, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I only suppose that this was a statement by Mladic rather than a debate between us. Particularly is in the same paragraph we fall to discussing the -- his soldiers that I have as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now his soldiers that you have as prisoners, how were they taken?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: They were taken by a French counterattack, after the French had had some soldiers killed and a position taken, in which the attackers dressed up at Frenchmen, Frenchmen in UN -- in the UN, and that is what I'm referring to in -- or is referred to as the breach of the protocols.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure if I understand what you mean by Frenchmen in the UN.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were in blue helmets and so forth. The bit that's the UN is the blue helmet. But the rest of it was in French uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, finally, I'd like that take a look at paragraph 12 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which will be found, I believe, on the next page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I am inferring something from the first sentence which is: "General Smith said he was not in command of NATO forces, nor did he direct their actions." So I'm inferring that what has happened is that Mladic has accused you of being responsible or in command of NATO forces and directing the bombing. And that's a question: Did he do that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Mladic says that he knew this was -- said he knew this to be a lie as NATO could not act without his request," referring to your request. And that's what I think you were talking about beforehand, where you requested the action be taken and then NATO then would proceed to do --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- the bombing?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you were the one responsible for recommending an attack take place, but you did not command the forces. Which would be correct from what you a have told us.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you -- did you collaborate with your colleagues in NATO as to what an appropriate target for the air-strike would be?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you inform them based upon the information that you had received as commander of UNPROFOR with regard to where particular sensitive targets would be?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not sure I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, when you collaborated with your colleagues about what would be an appropriate target --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I see what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't recall the basis on which the information came, whether it was my information or somebody else's, but we certainly discussed the targets, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And did you inform Mladic when you told him that you were not in control but that you had been responsible for recommending the attacks, that you had been instrumental in making a determination of what specific target would be under attack?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't think I told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not that was information that Mladic claimed to have intercepted?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Now, you also indicated -- you also took the opportunity to talk about different types of air action. Now, the first one, close air support, which was flown in direct support of the UN force which was used in self-defence, I take that would be where UNPROFOR unit had been specifically attacked?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The second type, which is air-strike, such as the two against the Bosnian Serbs last week," that was not one where there was a self-defence issue but, rather, that's what you would call -- if I might, a coercive act?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: You can call it what you will. That is the -- those air-strikes are the ones that associated with the exclusion zones that I discussed earlier in answer to one of your other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. And what I'm doing is I'm now taking that a bit further, which is that the determination to use an air-strike in a fashion other than in self-defence was the threat real -- was the threat realized, which is why I'm calling it a coercive act?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... no, no, it is associated with those exclusions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Enforcement of compliance. Is that what you want to say by --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just find out. The first category of self-defence, was self-defence in that sense limited only to an attack specifically against UNPROFOR forces, or could it be against third parties too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eight -- at the early part of the year, the interpretation was UNPROFOR or UNHCR and UNPROFOR, and an immediate threat, patent, immediate, present threat. As the year came on, and by later in the year this definition of self-defence becomes greatly enhanced, greatly expanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To include?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To include those under ones protection, so you are now starting to deal with people in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Safe zones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Safe areas, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, I'm done with that exhibit. Could we have P2364 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I want to refer specifically to paragraph 2(b) and discuss for a moment the issue of the Tuzla airfield. First of all, to your knowledge, were NATO forces used in improving the air strip at Tuzla in the calendar year of 1994?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think NATO was at all, no. Not in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were American personnel in the area of the Tuzla airport in 1994 with regard to determining the propriety and feasibility of using the Tuzla airport for potential NATO actions?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive any information with regard to such forces being in the area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When Mladic alleged the use of Tuzla airfield for the supply of arms to the BiH covered by NATO, I take it there he was referring to the BiH army; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Where -- where are we?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- yes, I would -- I think can you infer that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to -- with regard to your statement that is contained in this particular paragraph, when you told him that NATO was not in any way associated with the alleged landings of air-crafts at Tuzla, you did not disabuse him of the fact that aircraft were landing at Tuzla, did you?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I don't remember whether -- exactly what I'm responding to. But the -- I'm certainly and clearly stating there that NATO have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If NATO had nothing to do with it, to your knowledge, would the entity who was then using the Tuzla airfield be UNPROFOR and others, or who would it be?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: If it was being used, in -- whenever this is, March of 1995, it wasn't the UN, and it wasn't NATO. That's what I'm saying there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did the UN have any aircraft in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had some helicopters, and there was a number of aircraft used by Zagreb, but they didn't fly into Tuzla. They flew into Sarajevo and were still doing so in March of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These aircraft in Zagreb belonged to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: UN aeroplanes, yes. I mean, they were provided if my memory serves me correctly, by Ukraine, but they were, as it were, flying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under the UN flag.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to ask you just a very brief question with regard to a gentleman who I believe was on the ground before your time, and that was General Wahlgren. Did you ever have any contact with General Wahlgren?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do is I'd like to show you something and see whether or not you would agree with the statement made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have 1D00-2536 on the screen, and I'd like to have page 22. If we could go down to the -- scroll down. And you'll notice about midway in the very last paragraph it states: "General Wahlgren prophetically warned UN political authorities in New York, 'If one a allowed no controls of the military or paramilitary units of the Bosnian government, one would create a scenario which would encourage the use of the safe areas as havens where forces could refit, rearm, train, and prepare for further military operations.'" And I take it that that is the prophecy that you then were referring to when you said that there were BiH army members in the enclaves? And perhaps I'm being a bit more expansive than you would like to be.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: I think it is more of a prophecy of the hostage and shield situation. That's as I understand it. Can I be told what this comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. This comes from -- and if we can go to the very first page. It comes from an article entitled, "Responsibility of Command: How UN and NATO Commanders Influenced Air Power over Bosnia," written by Mark A. Bucknam of the United States air force, a colonel.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have for the moment, page 22 as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. With the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The cover page and page 22 of this document are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There came a time when a new coloured helmet was introduced into the area, the green helmets of the RFF?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Hardly new, but, yes, the rapid reaction force, I think is what you want, not the RFF.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: RRF.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The RRF was a force that was created to operate outside of the direct strictures of the rules of engagement that applied to UNPROFOR. True?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's a question.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. What was the purpose of the creation of the rapid reaction force?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First of all, who created it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who created the rapid reaction force it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It would be difficult to tie to down to a specific event and decision, but you see the beginnings of it being formed by me in the aftermath of the bombings at the end of May. And Britain and France, I requested some artillery and more forces, and Britain and France provide these. So you can probably date it from sometime in June as the origins of the force being designated, if you like. It then takes some time to appear, and it isn't formed up and complete until fairly late in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You had asked a question, and I interrupted, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, and I'm referring to once again your book, that you made the determination that: "In the event I was forbidden any offensive action, but the idea of the rapid reaction force gathered momentum in London and in Paris. And in early June it was agreed that such a force would deploy." And as you mentioned it would consist of French and British infantry. You go on to stay that: "The force was not to adopted UN blue helmets and paint their vehicles white. It was an unmarked UN force. This was fine by me. They were to fight, and I did foot want them to look like the UN. I particularly wanted the guns. In comparison with aircraft, guns were the appropriate -- appropriate target-locating and fire-control systems, apply fire as accurately, can maintain the fire for a longer, are not weather-dependant, and would be under my command. They could, in the right quantities and deployment, defeat the Bosnian Serb artillery." That's what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That's what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that you wanted this particular force which was not to adopt the UN blue helmets, would it be -- would it be fair to say that this force was going to operate under your guiding hand privately but not publicly?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It wasn't private. But it was -- it was -- it was eventually to become under my command. It did not, as I say, all get there, until after -- I'd have to look for the dates. But it's some time in August that I've got the lot there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. It's something that you did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. I'm not quite sure, are you objecting to the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Simply, if we could have the page number from the book that Mr. Guy-Smith has been reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. It's page 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Do we have the title of the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm not sure which one you want. It's page 354 and 355, and page 43 in e-court. I didn't scan the gentleman's entire book into the system. Although I thought about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have the title of the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour. It's 1D01-0620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The book is entitled "The Utility of Force: The Art of War in the Modern World." It's written by Rupert Smith, who is Britain's outstanding soldier of modern times, according to Mr. Keegan of the Daily Telegraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You indicated it wasn't private. You did not want Mladic to know that you controlled these forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to not wanting Mladic to know that you had these forces, meaning that you controlled these forces, what was the -- and I use the word in a positive, not a negative sense. What was the subterfuge or sleight of hand that you used to keep this information from Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: It wasn't to keep of information so much as to as to have him understand the information in a -- in a way to my advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So you were using -- would it be fair to say that you were using misinformation in order to --

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: This was entirely up to him to decide. This was an illusion, not deception, like a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thought that I said sleight of hand. I did.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: The answer to your question is that I tried wherever possible to make this force look as part of NATO and not part of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Were you concerned with the Bosnian Serb army's ability to obtain intelligence information regarding this plan?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Clearly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In that regard, what did -- what did you do to cloak the wolf in another kind of cloth?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: As you said, I didn't paint the vehicles white, and I didn't put blue helmets on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Five, four, three, two ... Would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering whether Mr. Guy-Smith can indicate how much longer he thinks he will be in cross-examination. Both parties had anticipated that this witness would finish today. And I'm wondering if Mr. Guy-Smith does not have a great deal more, whether perhaps we could either keep going, or could we sit for part of a session this afternoon, depending on the Court's schedule?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I was actually going to take the time to -- to go through my notes to see what I could -- what I could cut out. I don't think that I was -- I would be more than another hour. But whether -- I'm -- I don't want to commit right now, because there a couple of things I've just got to go through to make sure that I've ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm happy to do whatever the Chamber wishes to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can sit this afternoon, but 15 bis. One of us is not going to be available. Yeah, if everybody else is available. And I don't know whether there is a courtroom available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that -- I'm -- I was just informed that Lukic and Lukic is in here. I don't know about the other courtrooms, Your Honour. I don't know whether there is any availability. Rather than scrambling about, why don't we just do it first thing tomorrow morning and then proceed to base?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the Registrar is trying to make inquiries. We'll find out once she comes from the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Obviously I'm in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I'm advised that the courtroom is available. I don't know whether parties want to do. You have a Bench of 15 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- I am willing to proceed. I must admit that I'm a bit tired. I don't know whether the witness is similarly tired and would like to take a break or not. I have another witness to prepare for, for tomorrow. If I had my druthers I would prefer to start again tomorrow fresh, and hopefully I would be able to do it even in a shorter period of time than, my expectations are now, that we could have a full day. But I remain in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you're opposing Mr. Saxon's request, but you are in our hands. I'm not quite sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm opposing Mr. Saxon's request, but I also would in all fairness to Sir Rupert, I don't know whether or not he is a -- this is will cause him difficulties one way or the other. And I'm happy to take that into consideration. I have no desire to inconvenience anyone here, be it the Chamber or be it the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is that I have a sneaky suspicion that Mr. Saxon's request is based on his expectations of how things are going to unfold with the next witness tomorrow. And I think he is trying to reserve tomorrow to ensure that he can finish with the next witness, particularly it being the last day of -- or working week -- the last working day of the week for us tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is part of my concern, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe the -- is the next witness a 92 ter witness as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He is viva voce, I think. He is viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think they changed him again. I -- yesterday's viva voce is today's 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next witness will be led under Rule 92 ter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it is not this witness we have been told is coming. Well, we have a 92 ter witness here that we're not able to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There we are. So ... Do you still insist on coming back this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If Sir Rupert will not protest too much by coming back tomorrow morning, I had not insist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It looks like, Sir Rupert, you've got the key. I don't know whether it is single or double. Yeah, it's double, fatigue and convenience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fatigue is not a problem. I can go on answering questions; that shouldn't be a factor. I have arrangements, it being a public holiday in Belgium tomorrow and a child coming out of school on account of that, that makes me want to be in Brussels tomorrow morning, however late it is that I get there, so that would be my preference. I

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shall we then sit again this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll come back at quarter past two, and can we say in this court. And then Lukic and Lukic will be shifted. Court adjourned. Come back at a quarter past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.54 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, if you haven't finished in this one session, you're not likely to have other bite at the cherry. Everything, re-examination and all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. And it's my understanding that we're now sitting pursuant to 115 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Only 15 bis, not 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry 15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to just ask you very quickly what the letters MMB mean in relationship to the Rapid Reaction Force, if anything. Is that a term that you use for multi-national, something or other?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Ah. It -- it might -- if my -- I think what it refers to is that the force was formed under a brigade headquarters, which was called the multi-national brigade, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the force being formed under that particular brigade headquarters, was that, for the purposes that we've been discussing, so that it was not seemed to be under your direct control?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: That wasn't the reason for it, but it also helped to have that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, with regard to the Rapid Reaction Force, it was your assessment that the Rapid Reaction Force would be used to fight against the Bosnian Serb army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Not strictly, no. But it was -- it could have been used to fight against anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. But the most probable party was the Bosnian Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: They were the ones who were stopping me from doing what I was told to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They were getting in your way; correct?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Of discharging my mandated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to your understanding of the discharge of your mandate, would it be fair to say that there was a division of opinion between you and Janvier concerning whether or not negotiations would be fruitful?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: At what stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the May bombing.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. We did not agree on the way forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard, General Janvier believed that fighting could be prevented by negotiation; correct? In a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't think that was his belief. But I think he ought to speak for himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could refer the Court and counsel to page 17779.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which refers to a document that you were being asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page of what document actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a transcript of the proceedings in the Popovic case, and it's of Friday, the 9th of November, 2007. And I don't know whether or not -- you may not have that document, Your Honour, because the Prosecution may have only supplied you with information up to the 7th. So if could you have 1D01-1270 up. There were two other days of testimony. And if we could go to page 17779, which is page 27 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm picking up on the answer that you just give which was: "No, I don't think that was his belief, but I think he ought to speak for himself." You were asked to comment on a document, and it says, "General Smith," starting at line 10, "General Smith and Janvier have different opinions. General Janvier believes that it is possible to return to situation before 26 May through negotiations. General Smith does not believe that we can return to the situation, and the best we can hope for is the status quo." It continues at line 15: "General Smith also believes that this -- that," excuse me, "that is the parties -- that is the two parties want to fight and nothing will prevent them, not even UNPROFOR. General Janvier believes they can be prevented from fighting by negotiations." And you were asked the following question: "Does that fairly encapsulate the differences between you and your commander?" And your answer is: "Pretty well."

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, because of that difference of opinion with regard to how matters might proceed in the future, and by that I mean negotiation or fighting, you determined -- I'm sorry, I don't like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because he hasn't referred to fighting as -- as a resolution of the problem. Just nobody can stop them fighting, not even UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't mean to mischaracterize what you said there. Because of the differences of opinion, did you also, at that point, take it upon yourself to determine -- take it upon yourself to decide that you would make certain orders with or without the approval of your commander, Janvier?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT SMITH
utterances.text: No. He was my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
